title: Urban–Rural Differences in Clinical Characteristics and Visual Outcomes of Microincision Vitrectomy for Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy
content: Background/Objectives: To compare clinical characteristics and visual outcomes of microincision vitrectomy for proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) between urban and rural settings in Japan and examine factors associated with postoperative visual acuity. Methods: This retrospective study included 412 eyes of 312 patients who underwent 25-gauge vitrectomy between December 2020 and December 2025: 142 eyes of 112 patients in the urban setting and 270 eyes of 200 patients in the rural setting. Urban surgeons had 8 and 10 years of experience; the rural surgeon had 25 years. Best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was assessed ≥6 months postoperatively. Associations were examined using multivariable linear mixed-effects regression. Results: Compared with eyes in the urban group, those in the rural group had a higher prevalence of tractional retinal detachment (44.4% vs. 30.3%; P = 0.005), better mean postoperative BCVA (0.40 ± 0.67 vs. 0.63 ± 0.78 logMAR; P = 0.004), and a lower proportion with poor postoperative vision (BCVA ≥1.0 logMAR: 14.4% vs. 27.5%; P = 0.001). Higher preoperative intraocular pressure, worse BCVA in the affected and fellow eyes, and macular detachment were associated with worse postoperative BCVA. Vitreous hemorrhage and the combined rural-setting/25-year-surgeon-experience variable were associated with better postopera-tive BCVA (P = 0.0004 and P < 0.0001, respectively). Preoperative neovascular glaucoma also re-mained significant (P = 0.03). Conclusions: The rural group achieved better postoperative vision despite a higher prevalence of tractional retinal detachment. Geographic setting and surgeon expe-rience were confounded; their independent effects cannot be determined. Prospective studies de-signed to distinguish these effects are needed.
